      Chapter 18Contents

      Figures for papers, theses and assignments

      A chart that looks fine on screen can be blurry in print, unreadable at column width, or rejected by a journal's submission system. This chapter is a practical guide to getting figures out of Python as PNG, PDF, SVG or TIFF files, at the right size and resolution, and into Word, Google Docs, PowerPoint or LaTeX.

      18.1Raster vs vector: which format? Beginner

      Definitions

      Raster image: a grid of coloured pixels (PNG, JPEG, TIFF). It has a fixed resolution and becomes blurry or blocky when enlarged. Vector image: a description of shapes, lines and text (PDF, SVG, EPS). It stays perfectly sharp at any size and its text remains selectable.

      DPI (dots per inch): how many pixels are printed per inch of paper. A 3.5-inch-wide figure at 300 dpi is 1,050 pixels wide.

      Format Type Best for Avoid for
      PDF vector LaTeX papers and theses, journal submissions, printing very dense scatter plots (huge files): rasterise the points (see 18.4)
      SVG vector editing in Inkscape or Illustrator, Word 365, websites some older journal systems
      EPS vector journals that explicitly ask for it transparency (EPS doesn't support it)
      PNG raster, lossless Word, Google Docs, PowerPoint, websites, photos of plots enlarging after export
      TIFF raster, lossless journals that require TIFF for submission everyday use (very large files)
      JPEG raster, lossy photographs only charts: compression blurs lines and text
      TipThe two-file habit

      Save every final figure twice: a PDF (vector, for LaTeX, printing and later editing) and a 300-dpi PNG (for Word, slides and quick sharing). The function in section 18.6 does both in one call.

      18.2Size first, then resolution Beginner

      The most common mistake is making a figure at screen size and shrinking it into the paper, which makes the fonts tiny. Instead, create the figure at its final printed size and choose font sizes for that size.

      Target Width Typical font size
      Journal, single column 3.3–3.5 in (85–90 mm) 7–9 pt
      Journal, double column (full width) 6.7–7.2 in (170–183 mm) 7–9 pt
      A4 thesis or assignment, full text width about 6.3 in (160 mm) 9–11 pt
      Slide (16:9) 10–13 in 14–20 pt
      Poster panel 10–20 in 20+ pt

      Always check your journal's author guidelines; the numbers above are common defaults, not rules.

      18.3Saving with savefig: every option that matters Beginner

      Output
      PNG: 993 x 734 px  ->  3.31 x 2.45 in at 300 dpi

      Fonts that journals and Word accept Intermediate

      Output
      PDF has Type 3 fonts: False
      PitfallRequired fonts

      If a journal requires Arial or Helvetica, set plt.rcParams["font.family"] = "Arial". If Matplotlib can't find the font it falls back to another one and warns findfont: Font family 'Arial' not found. Install the font on your system, then delete Matplotlib's font cache (the folder shown by matplotlib.get_cachedir()) and restart Python.

      18.4Huge scatter plots: rasterise the points, keep the text sharp Intermediate

      A vector PDF with 100,000 points stores every point separately, which gives huge, slow files. Rasterising only the data layer keeps axes and text as vectors.

      Output
      scatter_raster_False.pdf 1448 KB
scatter_raster_True.pdf 110 KB

      18.5Multi-panel figures with panel letters Intermediate

      Journals usually want related plots combined into one figure with panels labelled a, b, c.

      18.7Exporting Seaborn and Plotly figures Beginner

      Library Code
      Matplotlib fig.savefig("f.pdf"), fig.savefig("f.png", dpi=300)
      Seaborn axes-level (histplot, boxplot, …) draw with ax=ax, then fig.savefig(...)
      Seaborn figure-level (relplot, displot, catplot, pairplot, jointplot) g = sns.relplot(...), then g.savefig("f.pdf")
      Plotly fig.write_image("f.png", width=700, height=450, scale=3), fig.write_image("f.pdf"), fig.write_html("f.html")
      pandas .plot() ax = df.plot(...), then ax.figure.savefig("f.png", dpi=300)

      For Plotly, the pixel size of a PNG is width × scale. For a 7-inch figure at 300 dpi you need 2,100 pixels: width=700, scale=3.

      18.8Putting figures into documents Beginner

      Destination Use How
      Microsoft Word PNG at 300 dpi (any version), or SVG (Word 365) Insert → Pictures → This Device. Right-click → Size and Position: set the width and keep "Lock aspect ratio" ticked. Don't stretch a small image larger.
      Google Docs PNG at 300 dpi Insert → Image → Upload from computer.
      PowerPoint / Keynote SVG (365) or high-resolution PNG Insert → Pictures. Make the figure at slide size with large fonts.
      LaTeX / Overleaf PDF Upload the PDF, then use the code below.
      Journal submission what the guidelines say (often PDF/EPS for plots, TIFF for images) Name files Figure1.pdf, Figure2.pdf, and keep the code that made them. 
      % LaTeX: include a vector PDF figure at full text width
\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/figure2.pdf}
  \caption{(a) Signal over time for three groups. (b) Score distributions;
           treated participants score higher.}
  \label{fig:results}
\end{figure}

      18.9Writing a good figure caption Beginner

      A caption should let a reader understand the figure without reading the main text:

      1. Title sentence stating what is shown, or better, the finding ("Treated participants scored higher than controls").
      2. What each panel shows (a, b, c).
      3. What the marks mean: error bars (SD, SEM or 95% CI?), shaded bands, dot sizes, colours.
      4. Sample sizes (n per group) and, if relevant, the statistical test.

      18.10Colour and accessibility Intermediate

      18.11Final-figure checklist Beginner

      • Made at the final printed size, with fonts of at least 7 pt at that size.
      • Axes labelled, with units; tick labels readable.
      • Colour-blind-safe palette, plus line styles or markers so it still works in grayscale.
      • Error bars and bands defined in the caption (SD, SEM or 95% CI), with n stated.
      • Saved as PDF (vector) and 300-dpi PNG; TIFF or EPS if the journal asks.
      • Fonts embedded (pdf.fonttype = 42); dense scatter layers rasterised.
      • Panel letters on multi-panel figures; consistent styling across all figures.
      • The code that generated it saved in your project, so it can be regenerated.

      3. Open your PNG in an image viewer and confirm its pixel width equals inches × dpi.

      Chapter 19Contents

      Machine-learning concepts and the scikit-learn API

      Before training any model you need a clear mental map: which kind of problem you have, how models learn, why we split data, and how to tell a model that generalises from one that has merely memorised. This chapter builds that map, then introduces the small, consistent API shared by every scikit-learn model.

      19.1The kinds of machine learning Beginner

      Definitions

      Machine learning: building models that learn patterns from data in order to make predictions or decisions, rather than following hand-written rules.

      Supervised learning: learning a mapping from features to a known target using labelled examples. It covers regression and classification.

      Unsupervised learning: finding structure, such as groups or lower-dimensional summaries, in data without a target variable.

      Regression: supervised learning where the target is a number (price, temperature).

      Classification: supervised learning where the target is a category (spam/not spam, species).

      Feature: an input variable used to make predictions; a column of X. Also called a predictor or covariate.

      Target (label): the variable a supervised model predicts; y.

      Sample (observation): one row of data: one patient, one image, one transaction.

      Hyperparameter: a setting chosen before training that controls how a model learns, such as tree depth or the regularisation strength C. It is not learned from the data.

      Type You have Goal Examples scikit-learn
      Supervised: regression features X and a numeric target y predict a number price, blood pressure, crop yield LinearRegression, RandomForestRegressor
      Supervised: classification X and a categorical y predict a class (and its probability) disease yes/no, species, spam LogisticRegression, RandomForestClassifier
      Unsupervised: clustering X only find groups customer segments, cell types KMeans, DBSCAN
      Unsupervised: dimensionality reduction X only compress or visualise PCA of gene expression PCA, TSNE
      Deep learning large X (images, text, signals) any of the above, with learned features image classification, forecasting TensorFlow / Keras (Part VI)

      Vocabulary you will see everywhere: a sample (row, observation, instance), a feature (column, variable, predictor), the target (label, response, outcome), training (fitting parameters to data), inference (predicting on new data), hyperparameters (settings you choose before training, such as tree depth), and parameters (values the model learns, such as regression coefficients).

      19.2The workflow at a glance Beginner

      19.3The estimator API: fit, predict, transform Beginner

      Definitions

      Estimator: any scikit-learn object that learns from data with fit(). Models (predict) and transformers (transform) are both estimators.

      Training (fitting): adjusting a model's parameters to the training data.

      Inference (prediction): using a trained model to produce outputs for new inputs.

      Every scikit-learn object follows the same small set of conventions:

      Method Available on What it does
      est = Model(**hyperparams) everything create the object; hyperparameters go here
      est.fit(X, y) everything learn from data; returns est itself
      est.predict(X) models predict targets for new samples
      est.predict_proba(X) most classifiers class probabilities, one column per class
      est.score(X, y) models default metric: accuracy (classifiers) or R² (regressors)
      est.transform(X) transformers (scalers, encoders, PCA) return a transformed version of X
      est.fit_transform(X) transformers fit and transform in one step (training data only!)
      est.attr_ fitted objects learned values end with _, e.g. coef_, classes_

      Data conventions: X is 2-D, shape (n_samples, n_features) (a DataFrame or array); y is 1-D, shape (n_samples,).

      Output
      (150, 4) (150,)
   sepal length (cm)  sepal width (cm)  petal length (cm)  petal width (cm)
0                5.1               3.5                1.4               0.2
1                4.9               3.0                1.4               0.2
2                4.7               3.2                1.3               0.2
accuracy: 0.9736842105263158
same via .score: 0.9736842105263158
[[1. 0. 0.]
 [0. 1. 0.]
 [0. 1. 0.]]
      Key ideaSwap one line, keep the rest

      Because every model shares this API, trying a different algorithm usually means changing only the line that creates it. That consistency is scikit-learn's greatest strength.

      Output
      LogisticRegression   test accuracy = 0.947
DecisionTree         test accuracy = 0.921
RandomForest         test accuracy = 0.895
SVC                  test accuracy = 0.921
GaussianNB           test accuracy = 0.921

      19.4Baselines: is the model actually learning anything? Beginner

      Definitions

      Baseline model: a deliberately trivial model, such as always predicting the mean or the most frequent class, that any useful model must beat.

      Always compare against a trivial baseline. A model that is "90% accurate" is useless if 90% of samples belong to one class.

      Output
      baseline accuracy: 0.316
mean-predictor R2: -0.0

      19.5Overfitting, underfitting and the bias–variance trade-off Beginner

      Definitions

      Overfitting: when a model learns noise in the training data, performing well on it but poorly on new data.

      Underfitting: when a model is too simple to capture the real pattern, performing poorly on training and new data alike.

      Bias–variance trade-off: simple models err systematically (high bias); flexible models vary a lot with the training sample (high variance). Good models balance the two.

      Generalisation: how well a model performs on new, unseen data, which is the goal of machine learning.

      A model underfits when it is too simple to capture the pattern (high bias): it is poor on training and test data alike. It overfits when it is so flexible that it memorises noise (high variance): excellent on training data, poor on new data. The goal is the sweet spot in between.

      Symptom Diagnosis Remedies
      train score low, test score low underfitting (high bias) more flexible model, better features, less regularisation, train longer
      train score high, test score much lower overfitting (high variance) more data, simpler model, more regularisation, feature selection, early stopping, ensembles
      train and test both high and close good fit confirm with cross-validation, then test once

      19.6Why the test set is sacred Beginner

      Definitions

      Training set: the data used to fit the model (and, via cross-validation, to choose among models).

      Validation set: data held out from training to tune hyperparameters and compare models.

      Test set: data locked away until the end and used once to estimate final performance on unseen data.

      The test set estimates how the model will perform on data it has never seen. Every time you use test results to make a decision (choose a model, tweak a feature, pick a threshold) you leak information from it into your modelling, and the final number becomes optimistic. Make all decisions with the training data, typically via cross-validation (Chapter 23), and evaluate on the test set once, at the end.

      Research practiceReport what the test set was used for

      In a paper, state how data were split (random, stratified, grouped by subject, by time), the split sizes, the random seed, and that the test set was used only once for the final evaluation. If you had to look at it more than once, say so.

      19.7Reproducibility knobs Beginner

      Many estimators and splitters are random. Pass random_state=<int> to make them deterministic: train_test_split(..., random_state=42), RandomForestClassifier(random_state=0), KFold(shuffle=True, random_state=0). Use a fixed integer; avoid relying on a global NumPy seed.

      Try it yourselfTry it yourself
      1. Load load_wine() and compare DummyClassifier, KNeighborsClassifier and RandomForestClassifier on a stratified split.
      2. In the polynomial demo, replace LinearRegression with Ridge(alpha=1e-3) for degree 15. What happens to the wiggles?
      3. Re-run the iris example with five different random_state values. How much does test accuracy vary? (This is why we cross-validate.)

      Chapter 20Contents

      Preprocessing, feature engineering and pipelines

      Models need numbers on sensible scales, with no missing values. Real tables have text categories, gaps and wildly different units. scikit-learn's transformers fix each of these problems, and a Pipeline chains them with a model so the whole thing is fitted correctly, without leakage, in one call.

      20.1Scaling numeric features Beginner

      Definitions

      Standardisation (z-scoring): rescaling a feature to mean 0 and standard deviation 1: (x − mean) / SD.

      Normalisation (min-max scaling): rescaling a feature to a fixed range, usually 0–1: (x − min) / (max − min).

      Transformer (scikit-learn): an estimator with fit and transform that changes data, such as a scaler, encoder or imputer.

      Distance-based and gradient-based models (kNN, SVM, logistic/linear regression with regularisation, neural networks, PCA) are sensitive to feature scale. Tree-based models (decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting) are not.

      Output
      StandardScaler  [-0.6  -0.55 -0.58  1.73]
MinMaxScaler    [0.   0.02 0.01 1.  ]
RobustScaler    [-0.06  0.02 -0.02  3.82]
learned mean_: [   2.5 1437.5]  scale_: [1.1000e+00 2.0571e+03]
[  1. 200.]
      Scaler Formula Use when
      StandardScaler (x − mean) / sd default choice; roughly symmetric features
      MinMaxScaler (x − min) / (max − min) you need a bounded range [0, 1], e.g. pixel intensities
      RobustScaler (x − median) / IQR features with outliers
      PowerTransformer / np.log1p makes skewed data more normal strongly right-skewed features (incomes, counts)
      PitfallFit on training data, transform both

      scaler.fit_transform(X_train) then scaler.transform(X_test). Never fit on the test set, and never fit on all data before splitting. A Pipeline enforces this for you.

      20.2Encoding categorical features Beginner

      Output
      [[0. 1. 0.]
 [0. 0. 1.]
 [1. 0. 0.]
 [0. 0. 1.]]
['region_east' 'region_north' 'region_south']
[[0. 0. 0.]]
[0. 2. 1. 1.]
      TipWhich encoder?

      Use one-hot for unordered categories (region, colour), ordinal for genuinely ordered ones (S < M < L, education level). Tree models also cope well with ordinal codes for unordered categories. For very high-cardinality columns (thousands of postcodes), consider TargetEncoder (it is cross-fitted internally to limit leakage) or grouping rare levels with OneHotEncoder(min_frequency=...).

      NoteModels that accept NaN directly

      HistGradientBoostingClassifier/Regressor, DecisionTree*, and RandomForest* in recent scikit-learn versions handle missing values natively. Most other estimators raise ValueError: Input X contains NaN.

      20.4Pipelines: preprocessing + model as one object Beginner

      Definitions

      Pipeline: a chain of preprocessing steps and a final model that is fitted and applied as one estimator, guaranteeing every step learns only from training data.

      A Pipeline is a list of steps. Calling fit runs fit_transform on each transformer, in order, then fit on the final model. Calling predict runs transform through each step, then predict. The fitted statistics always come from the data passed to fit.

      Output
      test accuracy: 0.958
[14.12 19.27 91.91]
['standardscaler', 'logisticregression']

      20.5ColumnTransformer: different processing per column Intermediate

      Definitions

      ColumnTransformer: a scikit-learn tool that applies different preprocessing to different groups of columns and joins the results.

      Real tables mix numeric and categorical columns. ColumnTransformer routes each group of columns through its own mini-pipeline and concatenates the results.

      Output
      (1000, 9)
['num__age' 'num__bmi' 'num__children' 'cat__sex_male' 'cat__smoker_yes'
 'cat__region_northeast' 'cat__region_northwest' 'cat__region_southeast'
 'cat__region_southwest']
      Output
      test R2: 0.9311
predicted charges: [19086.]
      TipSelect columns by type automatically

      make_column_selector(dtype_include="number") and make_column_selector(dtype_include=object) pick columns by dtype, so the preprocessor adapts when columns are added. In pandas 3, string columns match dtype_include=["object", "string"].

      20.6Seeing leakage with your own eyes Intermediate

      Definitions

      Data leakage: information from outside the training data (often from the test set or the target itself) influencing model training, which produces overly optimistic results.

      Here is why pipelines matter. We select the "best" features using all the data, then cross-validate on pure noise.

      Output
      selection outside CV: 0.85   <- looks impressive, entirely fake
selection inside CV : 0.48   <- honest: no signal
      Bug huntMy cross-validation score is great but the model fails on new data

      Classic leakage. Any step that learns from data (scaling, imputing, encoding with target information, feature selection, oversampling such as SMOTE, PCA) must happen inside the cross-validation loop, which means inside a Pipeline. Also check for duplicate rows across splits and for features that are computed from the target.

      20.7Feature engineering Intermediate

      Definitions

      Feature engineering: creating new, more informative features from raw data, such as ratios, logs, interactions, date parts and counts.

[[2. 3. 4. 6. 9.]] ['a' 'b' 'a^2' 'a b' 'b^2']

      Chapter 21Contents

      Regression: predicting numbers

      Regression models predict a continuous target. This chapter compares the main families (linear models, regularised linear models, nearest neighbours, trees and ensembles) on the insurance data, explains the metrics, and shows the diagnostic plots that tell you how a model is wrong.

      21.1Set-up: one preprocessor, many models Beginner

      Output
      (800, 6) (200, 6)

      21.2Regression metrics Beginner

      Definitions

      MAE (mean absolute error): the average size of prediction errors, in the target's units.

      RMSE (root mean squared error): the square root of the average squared error. It penalises large errors more than MAE.

      R² (coefficient of determination): the share of the target's variance explained by the model: 1 is perfect, 0 is no better than predicting the mean, negative is worse.

      Metric Formula (in words) Units Read it as
      MAE mean of |error| target units "on average we are off by this much"; robust to outliers
      RMSE square root of mean squared error target units penalises large errors more than MAE
      R² 1 − SSE / total variance none, at most 1 share of variance explained; 0 = as good as predicting the mean, negative = worse
      MAPE mean of |error| / |true| % relative error; unstable when true values are near 0

      21.3Linear models Beginner

      Definitions

      Linear regression: a model predicting the target as a weighted sum of the features plus an intercept, fitted by least squares.

      Coefficient: the weight a linear model gives a feature: the change in prediction per unit change in that feature, holding the others fixed.

      Regularisation: adding a penalty on model complexity (such as large coefficients) to reduce overfitting. L2 (Ridge) shrinks all coefficients; L1 (Lasso) can set some to exactly zero.

      Linear regression models the target as a weighted sum of features: ŷ = b + w₁x₁ + … + wₚxₚ. Regularisation adds a penalty on the size of the weights to reduce overfitting:

      • Ridge (L2) shrinks all coefficients toward zero; good when many features each matter a little.
      • Lasso (L1) can set coefficients exactly to zero, performing feature selection.
      • ElasticNet mixes both. alpha sets the penalty strength (higher = simpler model).
      Output
              model      MAE     RMSE     R2  MAPE%
Mean baseline 7296.699 9809.561 -0.011 35.173
       Linear 1821.972 2452.403  0.937  9.311
        Ridge 1813.913 2443.709  0.937  9.314
        Lasso 1822.076 2451.496  0.937  9.336
   ElasticNet 2562.295 3151.501  0.896 12.520

      Reading coefficients Intermediate

      Output
      cat__region_southeast     -220.0
cat__region_northeast      -95.0
cat__sex_male              -58.0
cat__region_northwest       19.0
cat__region_southwest      295.0
num__children              529.0
num__bmi                   883.0
num__age                  3446.0
cat__smoker_yes          23013.0
dtype: float64
intercept: 17126.0

      Because numeric features were standardised, each numeric coefficient means "change in charges for a one-standard-deviation increase". The smoker_yes coefficient is the estimated extra cost of smoking, holding the other features fixed.

      PitfallCoefficients are not causal effects

      Regression coefficients describe associations in this data, conditional on the other features in the model. They can change sign when correlated features are added or removed. For inference (confidence intervals, p-values) use statsmodels; scikit-learn focuses on prediction.

      The regularisation path Intermediate

      Output
                     model      MAE     RMSE     R2  MAPE%
               Ridge 1813.913 2443.709  0.937  9.314
               Lasso 1822.076 2451.496  0.937  9.336
              Linear 1821.972 2452.403  0.937  9.311
   Gradient boosting 1851.234 2515.920  0.933  9.427
       Random forest 1894.608 2573.662  0.930  9.708
HistGradientBoosting 1949.798 2606.751  0.929  9.927
           SVR (RBF) 1959.467 2711.818  0.923  9.916
      Tree (depth 5) 2062.774 2768.292  0.919 10.708
          ElasticNet 2562.295 3151.501  0.896 12.520
          kNN (k=10) 4227.245 6325.007  0.580 17.099
       Mean baseline 7296.699 9809.561 -0.011 35.173
      Key ideaSimple models first

      Why do linear models win here? The relationship in this data is almost linear: charges rise steadily with age and jump by a fixed amount for smokers. Flexible models have nothing extra to discover, and they pay for their flexibility with a little extra variance. On real data with interactions and thresholds the ranking often flips. You only find out by trying a baseline, a linear model and an ensemble, in that order. Note also how badly kNN does: with one-hot columns and few samples, "nearest neighbours" are not very near.

      How trees and ensembles work Intermediate

      Definitions

      Decision tree: a model that makes predictions by asking a sequence of yes/no questions about the features, ending in a leaf with a prediction.

      Ensemble: a model that combines many models' predictions, usually to improve accuracy and stability.

      Random forest: an ensemble of decision trees, each trained on a bootstrap sample with random subsets of features, whose predictions are averaged.

      Gradient boosting: an ensemble that adds shallow trees one at a time, each correcting the errors of the previous ones.

      • A decision tree splits the data with yes/no questions ("smoker?", "age < 43?") to make groups with similar targets. It is interpretable but overfits when deep.
      • A random forest averages hundreds of deep trees, each trained on a bootstrap sample with random feature subsets. Averaging cancels out much of the overfitting. It is robust and needs little tuning.
      • Gradient boosting builds shallow trees sequentially, each one correcting the errors of the ensemble so far. It is often the most accurate for tabular data, but more sensitive to hyperparameters (learning_rate, max_iter/n_estimators, max_depth). HistGradientBoosting* is scikit-learn's fast implementation for larger datasets, with native missing-value support. XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost are popular external libraries in the same family.
      Output
      |--- cat__smoker_yes <= 0.50
|   |--- num__age <= -0.14
|   |   |--- value: [13949.46]
|   |--- num__age >  -0.14
|   |   |--- value: [19912.88]
|--- cat__smoker_yes >  0.50
|   |--- num__age <= -0.28
|   |   |--- value: [36483.03]
|   |--- num__age >  -0.28
|   |   |--- value: [42618.71]

      21.5Diagnostic plots: how is the model wrong? Intermediate

      Definitions

      Residual: the difference between an observed value and the model's prediction (actual − predicted).

      TipSkewed targets

      Costs, incomes and counts are often right-skewed. Modelling log(y) can help linear models. In scikit-learn use TransformedTargetRegressor(regressor=pipe, func=np.log1p, inverse_func=np.expm1), so predictions and metrics come back in original units automatically.

      21.6Quantifying uncertainty in a test score Advanced

      Definitions

      Bootstrap: estimating the uncertainty of a statistic by recomputing it on many random resamples (drawn with replacement) of the data.

      Confidence interval (CI): a range that would contain the true value of a quantity in a stated share (often 95%) of repeated experiments.

      A single test RMSE is an estimate with sampling error. A bootstrap over test samples gives a confidence interval.

      Output
      RMSE = 2574  (95% CI 2159 to 3032)
      Research practiceReport intervals, not just point estimates

      "RMSE 2,574 (95% CI 2,159–3,032)" tells readers how much to trust the number, and whether two models' scores really differ. Chapter 30 covers comparing models rigorously.

      Try it yourselfTry it yourself
      1. Wrap the Ridge pipeline in TransformedTargetRegressor with a log transform and compare test RMSE.
      2. Add an interaction feature smoker × bmi (hint: PolynomialFeatures(interaction_only=True) or a custom column) to the linear model. Does it close the gap to the random forest?
      3. Plot test RMSE against max_depth from 1 to 15 for a single decision tree. Where does overfitting start?

      Chapter 22Contents

      Classification: predicting categories

      Classification models predict which class a sample belongs to, and usually how confident they are. Choosing the right metric matters more here than anywhere else in ML, because "accuracy" can be dangerously misleading. This chapter uses the Wisconsin breast-cancer dataset that ships with scikit-learn.

      22.1The data and a first model Beginner

      Output
      (569, 30) | malignant share: 0.373
accuracy: 0.986
first five probabilities: [1.    0.016 0.026 0.009 0.248]

      22.2The confusion matrix and the metrics built from it Beginner

      Definitions

      Confusion matrix: a table of predicted vs actual classes. For two classes it holds the true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives.

      Positive class: the class you want to detect (disease, fraud), coded 1. "Positive" means "the thing of interest", not "good".

      Accuracy: the share of all predictions that are correct.

      Precision: of the cases predicted positive, the share that really are positive: TP / (TP + FP).

      Recall (sensitivity): of the truly positive cases, the share the model detects: TP / (TP + FN).

      Specificity: of the truly negative cases, the share correctly identified: TN / (TN + FP).

      F1 score: the harmonic mean of precision and recall; high only when both are high.

      ROC curve and AUC: the ROC curve plots recall against the false-positive rate at every threshold; the area under it (AUC) is the probability that a random positive is ranked above a random negative.

      For a binary problem with a chosen "positive" class:

      Predicted negative Predicted positive
      Actually negative True Negative (TN) False Positive (FP), "false alarm"
      Actually positive False Negative (FN), "missed case" True Positive (TP)
      Metric Formula Question it answers
      Accuracy (TP+TN) / all What fraction is correct overall? Misleading with imbalanced classes.
      Precision TP / (TP+FP) When the model says positive, how often is it right?
      Recall (sensitivity, TPR) TP / (TP+FN) Of all real positives, how many did we catch?
      Specificity (TNR) TN / (TN+FP) Of all real negatives, how many did we correctly clear?
      F1 harmonic mean of precision and recall A single balance of the two.
      ROC AUC area under the ROC curve How well does the model rank positives above negatives (threshold-free)?
      PR AUC / average precision area under precision–recall curve Like ROC AUC, but more informative when positives are rare.
      Balanced accuracy mean of recall per class Accuracy that is fair under imbalance.
      MCC correlation between prediction and truth A robust single number for imbalanced binary problems (−1 to 1).
      Output
      TN=90 FP=0 FN=2 TP=51
precision=1.000  recall=0.962  F1=0.981  specificity=1.000
ROC AUC=0.9958  PR AUC=0.9940
balanced acc=0.981  MCC=0.970
              precision    recall  f1-score   support

      benign      0.978     1.000     0.989        90
   malignant      1.000     0.962     0.981        53

    accuracy                          0.986       143
   macro avg      0.989     0.981     0.985       143
weighted avg      0.986     0.986     0.986       143
      PitfallPassing labels where probabilities are needed

      roc_auc_score(y_te, y_pred) with hard 0/1 labels runs without error but gives a degraded, misleading AUC. Always pass predict_proba(X)[:, 1] (or decision_function(X)) to ROC AUC, average precision and log loss.

      22.3Visual evaluation: confusion matrix, ROC and PR curves Intermediate

      22.4Choosing the decision threshold Intermediate

      Definitions

      Decision threshold: the probability above which a classifier predicts the positive class (0.5 by default). Moving it trades precision against recall.

      predict() uses a probability threshold of 0.5, but nothing makes 0.5 special. In cancer screening a missed malignancy (FN) is far worse than a false alarm (FP), so we may accept more false alarms to raise recall.

      Output
      threshold 0.5: recall=0.962 precision=1.000 FN=2
threshold 0.3: recall=0.962 precision=0.895 FN=2
threshold 0.1: recall=1.000 precision=0.828 FN=0
      Output
      chosen threshold: 0.566
test balanced accuracy: 0.972
      Research practiceChoose the threshold on training/validation data

      Picking the threshold that looks best on the test set is another form of leakage. Tune it with cross-validation on the training data (as above), decide it from domain costs before looking at test results, or report threshold-free metrics (ROC AUC, PR AUC) alongside.

      22.5Comparing classifiers Intermediate

      Output
                   model  accuracy  recall  precision  ROC_AUC
LogisticRegression     0.986   0.962      1.000    0.996
         SVC (RBF)     0.951   0.943      0.926    0.993
     HistGradBoost     0.979   0.962      0.981    0.993
        ExtraTrees     0.958   0.962      0.927    0.992
      RandomForest     0.958   0.981      0.912    0.987
         kNN (k=7)     0.930   0.925      0.891    0.982
        GaussianNB     0.916   0.906      0.873    0.978
      DecisionTree     0.944   0.981      0.881    0.948
     Dummy (prior)     0.629   0.000      0.000    0.500
      PitfallOne split is a noisy judge

      With 143 test samples, one misclassification changes accuracy by 0.7 percentage points. Differences in the third decimal place are noise. Use cross-validation (Chapter 23) and confidence intervals (Chapter 30) before declaring a winner.

      Model Strengths Weaknesses Scale features?
      Logistic regression fast, interpretable coefficients, well-calibrated probabilities linear boundary unless you engineer features yes
      k-nearest neighbours no training, flexible boundary slow on big data, struggles in high dimensions yes
      SVM (RBF kernel) strong on small-to-medium data, flexible slow beyond ~10⁵ samples, needs C/gamma tuning yes
      Naive Bayes extremely fast, good for text strong independence assumption, poor probabilities no
      Decision tree readable rules unstable, overfits no
      Random forest / Extra trees robust defaults, little tuning, feature importance larger models, less interpretable no
      Gradient boosting often best on tabular data, handles NaN (Hist) more hyperparameters, can overfit no
      Neural network (Part VI) images, text, signals, huge data data-hungry, many design choices yes

      22.6Class imbalance Intermediate

      Definitions

      Class imbalance: when one class is much rarer than the others, which makes accuracy misleading and models biased toward the majority class.

      When one class is rare (fraud, rare disease), a model can score high accuracy by ignoring it.

      Output
      positive share in test: 0.033
dummy            acc=0.967  recall=0.000  precision=0.000  bal_acc=0.500
logreg           acc=0.967  recall=0.000  precision=0.000  bal_acc=0.500
logreg balanced  acc=0.762  recall=0.650  precision=0.088  bal_acc=0.708
      TipImbalance toolbox
      1. Use the right metrics: recall, precision, F1, PR AUC, balanced accuracy, MCC. 2. Stratify every split (stratify=y, StratifiedKFold). 3. Use class_weight="balanced" where available. 4. Tune the decision threshold. 5. Resampling (SMOTE, undersampling) is available in the imbalanced-learn package; resample only inside training folds, using its imblearn.pipeline.Pipeline.

      22.7Probability calibration Advanced

      Definitions

      Calibration: how well predicted probabilities match observed frequencies: among cases given 80%, about 80% should be positive.

      A model is calibrated if, among samples given probability 0.8, about 80% are truly positive. This matters whenever probabilities feed decisions or risk scores.

      22.8Multiclass problems Intermediate

      Output
      [[15  0  0]
 [ 0 18  0]
 [ 0  0 12]]
macro F1: 1.0 | weighted F1: 1.0
one-vs-rest ROC AUC: 1.0
      Bug huntValueError: Target is multiclass but average='binary'

      precision_score, recall_score and f1_score default to average="binary". For three or more classes pass average="macro", "weighted" or "micro". For string labels in a binary problem, pass pos_label="yes" (or whichever is positive).

      Try it yourselfTry it yourself
      1. Find the threshold that gives at least 98% recall on the training data via cross-validated probabilities (cross_val_predict(..., method="predict_proba")) and report test precision at that threshold.
      2. Repeat the imbalance experiment with HistGradientBoostingClassifier(class_weight="balanced").
      3. Plot ROC curves of three models on one axes by passing the same ax to each RocCurveDisplay.

      Chapter 23Contents

      Model selection: cross-validation and hyperparameter tuning

      A single train/test split gives one noisy number. Cross-validation gives a more reliable estimate and lets you compare models and tune hyperparameters without touching the test set. This chapter covers the CV strategies you will need in research, including grouped and time-ordered data, then grid search, random search, learning curves and nested cross-validation.

      23.1k-fold cross-validation Beginner

      Definitions

      Cross-validation (CV): repeatedly splitting the training data into fitting and validation parts and averaging the scores, for a more reliable performance estimate.

      Fold: one of the k parts the data is divided into in k-fold cross-validation.

      Stratification: splitting data so that each part keeps the same class proportions as the whole.

      The training data is split into k folds. The model is trained k times, each time holding out a different fold for validation. You get k scores, so you can report a mean and a spread.

      Output
      [0.9933 0.9969 0.9886 0.9943 0.9995] mean=0.9945 sd=0.0036
fit_time          0.0028
score_time        0.0035
test_accuracy     0.9780
train_accuracy    0.9901
test_roc_auc      0.9947
train_roc_auc     0.9981
test_f1           0.9825
train_f1          0.9921
dtype: float64
      TipScoring names

      scoring= accepts strings such as "accuracy", "balanced_accuracy", "f1", "f1_macro", "roc_auc", "average_precision", "neg_log_loss", "r2", "neg_mean_absolute_error", "neg_root_mean_squared_error". Error metrics are negated so that "higher is better" always holds; flip the sign when reporting. sklearn.metrics.get_scorer_names() lists them all.

      Output
      50 scores: mean=0.9940, 2.5–97.5 percentile = 0.9763–1.0000

      23.2Choosing the right splitter Intermediate

      The CV scheme must mimic how the model will be used. Getting this wrong is the most common reason published ML results fail to replicate.

      Data situation Splitter Why
      i.i.d. rows, regression KFold(shuffle=True) standard
      i.i.d. rows, classification StratifiedKFold(shuffle=True) keeps class balance in each fold
      several rows per subject/patient/site GroupKFold, StratifiedGroupKFold the same subject must never appear in both train and validation
      time series / forecasting TimeSeriesSplit always train on the past, validate on the future
      very small datasets LeaveOneOut, RepeatedStratifiedKFold use every sample, reduce variance

      Grouped data: the leakage you don't see Intermediate

      Output
      KFold accuracy:      0.88  <- the model recognises subjects it has already seen
GroupKFold accuracy: 0.49  <- honest: near chance
      Research practiceIf you have multiple samples per subject, group by subject

      Patients with several scans, participants with several trials, sites with many plots, molecules with several conformers: the unit of generalisation is the subject, so the split must be by subject. Report it explicitly in your Methods.

      Time series Intermediate

      Output
      fold 0: train 0–19  validate 20–29
fold 1: train 0–29  validate 30–39
fold 2: train 0–39  validate 40–49
fold 3: train 0–49  validate 50–59

      23.3Hyperparameter tuning with GridSearchCV Intermediate

      Definitions

      Hyperparameter tuning: searching for the hyperparameter values that give the best cross-validated performance.

      Grid search: trying every combination of hyperparameter values from a predefined grid. Random search samples combinations at random instead.

      GridSearchCV tries every combination in a grid, scores each with cross-validation, and refits the best one on the whole training set.

      Output
      best params: {'svc__C': 1, 'svc__gamma': 'scale', 'svc__kernel': 'rbf'}
best CV ROC AUC: 0.9966
test ROC AUC (once!): 0.9934
 param_svc__C param_svc__gamma  mean_test_score  std_test_score  rank_test_score
          1.0            scale           0.9966          0.0045                1
          1.0             0.01           0.9962          0.0052                2
         10.0            scale           0.9962          0.0046                2
         10.0             0.01           0.9956          0.0059                4
        100.0            0.001           0.9954          0.0060                5

      Searching over models and preprocessing too Advanced

      A grid can be a list of dicts, and a pipeline step can itself be a hyperparameter.

      Output
      RandomForestClassifier(random_state=0) 0.9958

      23.4RandomizedSearchCV and successive halving Intermediate

      When there are many hyperparameters, sampling random combinations from distributions finds good settings with far fewer fits than a full grid.

      Output
      {'l2_regularization': 5.2329, 'learning_rate': 0.0692, 'max_leaf_nodes': 39, 'min_samples_leaf': 6}
best CV ROC AUC: 0.993
      TipBeyond random search

      HalvingGridSearchCV / HalvingRandomSearchCV (enable with from sklearn.experimental import enable_halving_search_cv) discard poor candidates early. Optuna performs Bayesian optimisation and integrates well with scikit-learn and Keras.

      23.5Learning curves and validation curves Intermediate

      Definitions

      Learning curve: training and validation scores plotted against training-set size; it shows whether more data would help.

      Validation curve: training and validation scores plotted against one hyperparameter; it shows under- and overfitting.

      23.6Nested cross-validation: an unbiased estimate after tuning Advanced

      Definitions

      Nested cross-validation: an outer CV loop that estimates performance, with an inner CV loop inside each outer fold that tunes hyperparameters.

      search.best_score_ is optimistically biased, because the same folds were used to choose the hyperparameters. When you have no separate test set (common with small research datasets), wrap the search inside an outer CV loop.

      Output
      non-nested best_score_: 0.9960
nested CV estimate:     0.9968 ± 0.0054

      Here the two numbers agree closely: the dataset is easy and the grid is small, so there is little room for the search to overfit the folds. With large search spaces, small samples or noisy targets the non-nested score can be inflated by several points, and you cannot know in advance which situation you are in.

      Research practiceWhich number goes in the paper?

      Report the nested CV score (or the score on an untouched test set) as your performance estimate, never best_score_ from the same search. Report the hyperparameter search space and the selection metric, so others can reproduce the tuning.

      Try it yourselfTry it yourself
      1. Tune n_neighbors (1–30) and weights ("uniform", "distance") for kNN on the breast-cancer data with GridSearchCV.
      2. Use cross_validate(..., return_estimator=True) to inspect how much logistic-regression coefficients vary across folds.
      3. Compare 5-fold and 10-fold CV estimates and their standard deviations for the same model.

      Chapter 24Contents

      Unsupervised learning: clustering and dimensionality reduction

      Without a target variable, the questions change: are there natural groups in the data? Can its many dimensions be summarised by a few? Unsupervised methods answer these questions, and they are also essential tools for exploring data before supervised modelling.

      24.1k-means clustering Beginner

      Definitions

      Clustering: grouping observations so that those in the same group (cluster) are more similar to each other than to those in other groups.

      k-means: a clustering algorithm that places k centres and alternately assigns points to the nearest centre and moves each centre to the mean of its points.

      Centroid: the centre (mean position) of a cluster.

      k-means places k centres and assigns every point to its nearest centre, then moves each centre to the mean of its points, repeating until nothing changes. It finds compact, roughly spherical clusters of similar size.

      Output
      inertia (within-cluster sum of squares): 20.89
cluster sizes: [125 125 125 125]

      Choosing k: elbow and silhouette Intermediate

      Definitions

      Inertia: the sum of squared distances from each point to its cluster centre. Lower means tighter clusters.

      Silhouette score: for each point, how much closer it is to its own cluster than to the next nearest one, averaged. It runs from −1 to 1; higher is better.

      Output
      best k by silhouette: 4
      PitfallClusters always "exist"

      k-means will happily split pure noise into k groups. Validate clusters: check stability across random seeds and subsamples, inspect what distinguishes them (profile the features per cluster), and ask whether they mean anything in your domain.

      24.2Other clustering algorithms Intermediate

      Algorithm Finds Need to set Notes
      KMeans spherical, similar-sized clusters n_clusters fast; scale features; MiniBatchKMeans for big data
      GaussianMixture elliptical clusters, soft membership n_components choose by BIC/AIC (.bic(X))
      DBSCAN / HDBSCAN arbitrary shapes, labels noise eps, min_samples (HDBSCAN: min_cluster_size) no k needed; struggles with varying density (HDBSCAN copes better)
      AgglomerativeClustering hierarchy of clusters n_clusters or distance_threshold, linkage dendrograms via SciPy

      Evaluating clusters when labels exist Intermediate

      Output
      ARI: 1.0
NMI: 1.0
silhouette: 0.821

      24.3Principal component analysis (PCA) Intermediate

      Definitions

      Dimensionality reduction: representing data with fewer features while keeping as much useful information as possible.

      PCA (principal component analysis): finding new, uncorrelated axes (principal components) that capture the most variance, ordered from most to least.

      Explained variance ratio: the share of the total variance captured by each principal component.

      PCA finds new axes (principal components) that are uncorrelated linear combinations of the original features, ordered by how much variance they capture. Keeping the first few gives a compact summary of the data.

      Output
      variance explained by PC1, PC2: [0.443 0.19 ]
components for 95% variance: 10
      Output
      mean concave points     0.261
mean concavity          0.258
worst concave points    0.251
mean compactness        0.239
worst perimeter         0.237
Name: PC1, dtype: float64
      Output
      CV accuracy with PCA: 0.9807

      24.4t-SNE and UMAP for visualisation Advanced

      Definitions

      t-SNE / UMAP: non-linear methods that map high-dimensional data to 2-D or 3-D for visualisation, preserving local neighbourhoods.

      PCA is linear. t-SNE (and the popular external package UMAP) produce non-linear 2-D maps that preserve local neighbourhoods. They are excellent for looking at high-dimensional data, such as images, embeddings or single-cell data.

      PitfallDon't over-read t-SNE plots

      Distances between clusters and cluster sizes in t-SNE/UMAP maps are not meaningful, and the layout changes with perplexity and seed. Use them to explore, never as evidence by themselves; don't cluster on t-SNE coordinates or feed them to a model.

      24.5Anomaly detection Intermediate

      Definitions

      Anomaly detection: identifying observations that differ markedly from the majority, such as fraud, faults or rare events.

      Output
      flagged: 16 | of the true anomalies caught: 12 / 15
      Try it yourselfTry it yourself
      1. Cluster the insurance customers (scaled age, bmi, charges) with k-means and profile each cluster with groupby(labels).mean().
      2. Run PCA on the wine dataset and plot the first two components coloured by cultivar.
      3. Compare t-SNE maps of the digits with perplexity 5, 30 and 100.

      Chapter 25Contents

      Interpreting, explaining and saving models

      A model that predicts well is only half the job in research. Reviewers and colleagues will ask which features matter, how they affect predictions, and whether the model can be reused. This chapter covers built-in importances and their pitfalls, permutation importance, partial dependence, SHAP, and persisting models safely.

      25.1Set-up Beginner

      Output
      test R2: 0.928

      25.2Impurity-based feature importance Intermediate

      Definitions

      Feature importance: a score of how much a model relies on each feature.

      Tree ensembles expose feature_importances_: how much each feature reduced the splitting criterion, summed over all trees. It is free to compute but has known biases.

      Output
      smoker_yes          0.8407
age                 0.1266
bmi                 0.0182
noise               0.0065
children            0.0036
sex_male            0.0015
region_southwest    0.0012
region_northeast    0.0007
region_southeast    0.0007
region_northwest    0.0005
dtype: float64
      PitfallImpurity importance is biased

      It is computed on training data, and it favours continuous, high-cardinality features, which offer many possible split points. Notice that the pure-noise column outranks children, sex and every region column above. Prefer permutation importance on held-out data for conclusions.

      25.3Permutation importance Intermediate

      Definitions

      Permutation importance: the drop in a model's score when one feature's values are randomly shuffled, which breaks its link with the target.

      Shuffle one feature's values in the test set and measure how much the score drops. If the model relied on that feature, performance falls; if not, nothing changes. It is model-agnostic and computed on held-out data.

      Output
                  mean      sd
smoker    1.6078  0.1436
age       0.2830  0.0224
bmi       0.0232  0.0035
children  0.0053  0.0013
sex       0.0002  0.0005
region    0.0002  0.0006
noise    -0.0000  0.0014
      NoteCorrelated features share importance

      If two features carry the same information, shuffling one barely hurts because the model uses the other. Both then look unimportant. Check correlations first, and consider permuting correlated groups together.

      25.4Partial dependence and ICE plots Intermediate

      Definitions

      Partial dependence plot (PDP): the model's average prediction as one feature varies, with the other features averaged out.

      ICE plot (individual conditional expectation): one line per sample showing how its prediction changes as one feature varies.

      A partial dependence plot (PDP) shows the average predicted outcome as one feature varies, averaging over the others. ICE lines show the same for individual samples, revealing heterogeneity.

      NoteCategorical features in partial dependence

      For a categorical feature on its own, pass categorical_features=["smoker"] to get a bar per category. Two-way plots that mix a continuous and a categorical feature are not supported. Instead, draw one-way ICE plots coloured by group, or compare PDPs computed on each subgroup.

      25.5SHAP values Advanced

      Definitions

      SHAP value: the contribution of one feature to one prediction, based on Shapley values from game theory. A sample's SHAP values add up to its prediction minus the average prediction.

      SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) splits each individual prediction into additive contributions from each feature, grounded in cooperative game theory. It gives both local explanations (one prediction) and global summaries. It lives in the separate shap package (pip install shap).

      Research practiceInterpretation claims need care

      Importance and SHAP describe the model, not the world. A feature can be important because it is a proxy for something else, because of leakage, or because of a quirk of the sample. Validate interpretations with domain knowledge, stability across CV folds and seeds, and if possible on external data. Avoid causal language ("X causes Y") unless your design supports it.

      25.6Saving and loading models Beginner

      Definitions

      Serialization: saving an object, such as a fitted model, to a file so it can be loaded later. joblib and pickle do this in Python.

      Save the whole fitted pipeline, so preprocessing travels with the model.

      Output
      True
{'sklearn': '1.9.1', 'python': '3.13.18', 'features': ['age', 'sex', 'bmi', 'children', 'smoker', 'region', 'noise'], 'test_r2': 0.928}
      PitfallPickles are version-specific and unsafe

      A model saved with one scikit-learn version may not load (or may behave differently) under another, so record versions as above. Never load a .joblib/.pkl file from an untrusted source: unpickling can execute arbitrary code. For long-term or cross-language deployment, consider the skops format or exporting to ONNX (skl2onnx).

      Bug huntValueError: The column 0 contains integer data. Partial dependence plots are not supported for integer data

      Recent scikit-learn versions refuse to compute partial dependence on integer columns, because the grid of values would be silently rounded. Convert those columns to float first: X = X.astype({"age": float}). That is why the set-up code above casts age and children.

      Try it yourselfTry it yourself
      1. Compute permutation importance with scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error". Does the ranking change?
      2. Draw ICE plots for children. Is the effect the same for everyone?
      3. Save a fitted pipeline, restart Python, load it, and predict for a brand-new customer DataFrame.

      Chapter 26Contents

      TensorFlow fundamentals: tensors, gradients and data pipelines

      TensorFlow is a library for numerical computing on CPUs, GPUs and TPUs with automatic differentiation: it can compute the gradient of any calculation you write. Keras, its high-level API, builds neural networks from layers. This chapter covers the low-level pieces that every Keras model is made of, so that the next chapters (and their error messages) make sense.

      NoteInstallation and hardware

      pip install tensorflow installs a CPU build that runs everywhere; GPU support on Linux is pip install "tensorflow[and-cuda]". On Windows, use WSL2 for GPU training. Everything in this part runs comfortably on a laptop CPU.

      26.1Tensors Beginner

      Definitions

      Tensor: TensorFlow's n-dimensional array, with a shape and a dtype, that can live on a CPU, GPU or TPU.

      GPU: a graphics processor with thousands of small cores, which speeds up the matrix maths of deep learning enormously.

      A tensor is TensorFlow's n-dimensional array, very much like a NumPy array, with a shape and a dtype.

      Output
      TensorFlow 2.21.0
tf.Tensor(
[[1. 2.]
 [3. 4.]], shape=(2, 2), dtype=float32)
(2, 2) <dtype: 'float32'> 2
(2, 3) [1. 1. 1.] <dtype: 'float32'>
<dtype: 'int64'> <dtype: 'float32'>
      Pitfallfloat32 is the default for deep learning

      tf.constant([1.0]) is float32, but NumPy arrays default to float64. Mixing them raises InvalidArgumentError: cannot compute AddV2 as input #1(zero-based) was expected to be a float tensor but is a double tensor. Convert data with X.astype("float32").

      26.2Operations Beginner

      Output
      tf.Tensor(
[[11. 12. 13.]
 [14. 15. 16.]], shape=(2, 3), dtype=float32)
tf.Tensor(
[[ 1.  4.  9.]
 [16. 25. 36.]], shape=(2, 3), dtype=float32)
tf.Tensor(
[[14. 32.]
 [32. 77.]], shape=(2, 2), dtype=float32)
tf.Tensor(21.0, shape=(), dtype=float32) [2.5 3.5 4.5]
(3, 2) (1, 2, 3)
[2. 5.] [2 2]
[0.659 0.242 0.099]

      26.3Variables and automatic differentiation Intermediate

      Definitions

      Automatic differentiation (autodiff): computing exact derivatives of any calculation automatically, by recording its operations. tf.GradientTape does this.

      tf.Variable: a tensor whose value can change, used for model weights.

      Optimizer: the algorithm that updates the weights using the gradients, such as SGD or Adam.

      A tf.Variable holds a value that can change, such as a weight. tf.GradientTape records the operations performed inside it, and can then compute gradients of a result with respect to any variable.

      Output
      15.0 8.0
[ 0.5403 -0.4161 -0.99  ] [ 0.5403 -0.4161 -0.99  ]

      Training a model by hand Intermediate

      This is what model.fit() does under the hood: predict, compute the loss, compute gradients, and let an optimiser update the weights.

      Output
      learned slope=2.973, intercept=1.984, final loss=0.0417

      26.4Speed: tf.function Advanced

      Decorating a Python function with @tf.function compiles it into a TensorFlow graph, which usually runs faster and can be exported. Keras does this for you inside fit().

      Output
      0.0416865348815918
      Bug huntPython side-effects inside tf.function

      print() inside a tf.function runs only while the function is being traced (usually once), not on every call; use tf.print() instead. Avoid changing Python lists or global variables inside it. While debugging, run eagerly with tf.config.run_functions_eagerly(True).

      26.5Input pipelines with tf.data Intermediate

      Definitions

      Mini-batch: a small subset of the training data (such as 32 samples) used for one gradient update.

      tf.data.Dataset streams data in shuffled mini-batches, applies transformations in parallel, and prefetches the next batch while the model trains. It scales from NumPy arrays to datasets far larger than memory.

      Output
      (32, 4) (32,) [0 1 0 1 0 0 0 1]
batches per epoch: 32
      TipWhen to use tf.data

      For small in-memory tables, passing NumPy arrays straight to model.fit(X, y, batch_size=32) is simplest. Reach for tf.data for large datasets, images on disk (tf.keras.utils.image_dataset_from_directory), text, or heavy on-the-fly augmentation.

      26.6Reproducibility Beginner

      Output
      [0.6646 0.441  0.3529]
[0.6646 0.441  0.3529]
      Research practiceDeterminism on GPUs

      Some GPU operations are non-deterministic even with seeds. For bit-exact reruns call tf.config.experimental.enable_op_determinism() (slower). In practice, report the mean and standard deviation over several seeds: deep-learning results vary run to run.

      Try it yourselfTry it yourself
      1. Use GradientTape to find the minimum of f(x) = (x − 4)² + 1 by gradient descent, starting from x = 0.
      2. Extend the manual training loop to two input features.
      3. Build a tf.data pipeline from the breast-cancer data (load_breast_cancer) with batches of 64.

      Chapter 27Contents

      Neural networks with Keras

      A neural network is a stack of layers. Each dense layer computes activation(X @ W + b), and stacking several with non-linear activations lets the network learn complex functions. Keras turns this into a few lines: define, compile, fit, evaluate. This chapter builds classifiers and regressors on tabular data, then covers the tools for controlling training: callbacks, regularisation and saving.

      27.1The Keras workflow in five steps Beginner

      Definitions

      Neural network: a model made of layers of simple units (neurons). Each unit computes a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias and passes it through an activation function.

      Layer: a building block of a neural network that transforms its input. A dense (fully connected) layer connects every input to every unit.

      Activation function: the non-linear function applied by a unit, such as ReLU (max(0, z)), sigmoid or softmax. It lets networks learn non-linear patterns.

      MLP (multilayer perceptron): a neural network made of stacked dense layers.

      Weights and biases: the learnable parameters of a layer: weights scale the inputs, biases shift the result.

      Output
      (364, 30) (91, 30) (114, 30)

      27.2Choosing the output layer and loss Beginner

      This table prevents the most common Keras mistakes.

      Task Output layer Loss Labels look like
      Binary classification Dense(1, activation="sigmoid") "binary_crossentropy" 0/1, shape (n,)
      Multiclass, integer labels Dense(k, activation="softmax") "sparse_categorical_crossentropy" 0…k−1, shape (n,)
      Multiclass, one-hot labels Dense(k, activation="softmax") "categorical_crossentropy" shape (n, k)
      Multi-label (several can be true) Dense(k, activation="sigmoid") "binary_crossentropy" 0/1 matrix (n, k)
      Regression Dense(1) (no activation) "mse", "mae", "huber" real numbers
      Bug huntAccuracy stuck around chance, or a shape error about logits and labels

      Usually the output/loss/labels don't match. Examples: softmax with 2 units but binary_crossentropy; integer labels with categorical_crossentropy (use sparse_...); or Dense(1) without sigmoid for a classifier. If your last layer has no activation, pass from_logits=True to the loss, e.g. keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True).

      27.3Callbacks: early stopping, checkpoints, learning-rate schedules Intermediate

      Definitions

      Callback: a function Keras calls automatically during training, for example at the end of each epoch, to stop early, save the model or change the learning rate.

      Early stopping: ending training when validation performance stops improving, to prevent overfitting.

      Dropout: randomly switching off a fraction of units during each training step, which forces the network to be robust and reduces overfitting.

      Output
      stopped after 61 epochs
test accuracy: 0.9649

      Regularisation compared Intermediate

      Technique Keras Effect
      Early stopping callbacks.EarlyStopping stop before overfitting; nearly always use it
      Dropout layers.Dropout(0.2–0.5) randomly removes units in training; reduces co-adaptation
      L2 / L1 weight penalty kernel_regularizer=regularizers.l2(1e-4) keeps weights small
      Batch normalisation layers.BatchNormalization() stabilises and speeds up training of deeper nets
      Data augmentation layers.RandomFlip, RandomRotation, … more varied training data (images)
      Smaller network fewer units/layers less capacity to memorise

      27.4Multiclass classification Intermediate

      Output
      [[0.001 0.001 0.998]
 [0.659 0.336 0.005]
 [0.    0.998 0.001]] [1.        0.9999999 1.       ]
test accuracy: 1.0
      Pitfallvalidation_split takes the last rows

      validation_split=0.2 uses the final 20% of the arrays before shuffling. If your data is sorted (by class, date or subject), shuffle first or pass an explicit validation_data=(X_val, y_val).

      27.5Regression Intermediate

      Output
      test RMSE = 1,997   MAE = 1,603  (charges)

      The MLP does well here, but this split (missing rows dropped, a different seed) differs from Chapter 21's, so the numbers cannot be ranked against each other. Compare models only under the same cross-validation protocol. As a rule, for tabular data, gradient boosting and linear models are strong baselines that neural networks often fail to beat. Deep learning shines on images, audio, text and very large datasets.

      27.6The Functional API Advanced

      Sequential handles single-input, single-output stacks. The Functional API builds any graph of layers: multiple inputs, multiple outputs, skip connections.

      Output
      ['numeric', 'category'] (None, 1) 162

      27.7Saving and loading Beginner

      Output
      True
      Research practiceSave the scaler too

      A Keras model expects inputs scaled exactly as in training. Save the fitted StandardScaler with joblib.dump(scaler, "scaler.joblib") next to the model, or put preprocessing inside the model with layers.Normalization (call .adapt(X_train) on it before training).

      Try it yourselfTry it yourself
      1. Replace the two hidden layers with one layer of 8 units. Does test accuracy change? What about 256 units?
      2. Add layers.BatchNormalization() after each Dense layer and compare the training curves.
      3. Wrap build_model in a loop over five seeds and report test accuracy as mean ± SD.

      Chapter 28Contents

      Deep learning architectures: CNNs, sequence models and custom training

      Dense networks treat every input as an unrelated number. Convolutional networks (CNNs) exploit the spatial structure of images; recurrent and 1-D convolutional networks exploit order in sequences. This chapter builds both on small datasets that train in seconds on a CPU, then shows custom training loops and transfer learning.

      28.1Convolutional neural networks Intermediate

      Definitions

      Convolutional neural network (CNN): a network that slides small learnable filters over its input to detect local patterns. It is the standard architecture for images.

      Convolution: sliding a small filter (kernel) over the input and computing a weighted sum at each position, producing a feature map.

      Pooling: downsampling a feature map, for example by keeping the maximum in each 2 × 2 block, which reduces size and adds robustness to small shifts.

      Channel: one layer of values in an image tensor: 1 for grayscale, 3 for RGB, or many feature maps inside a CNN.

      A convolution layer slides small learnable filters (for example 3×3) across the image. Each filter detects a local pattern, such as an edge, wherever it appears. Pooling layers downsample, so deeper layers see larger regions. A typical CNN: [Conv → Pool] × n → Flatten → Dense → output.

      Output
      (1437, 8, 8, 1) (360, 8, 8, 1) [142 146 142 146 145 145 145 143 139 144]
      Output
      Model: "sequential_7"
┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓

      Data augmentation Intermediate

      Definitions

      Data augmentation: creating varied training examples by randomly transforming existing ones (rotations, flips, crops) while keeping their labels.

      Augmentation layers randomly transform training images (flip, rotate, zoom, shift), effectively enlarging the dataset. They are active only during training.

      Output
      (5, 8, 8, 1)
      TipChoose augmentations that preserve the label

      Horizontal flips are fine for cats and chest X-rays (with care), wrong for digits and text. Rotations are fine for microscopy, wrong for street signs. Augmentation encodes your assumptions about which changes don't matter.

      28.2Transfer learning Advanced

      Definitions

      Transfer learning: starting from a model pretrained on a large dataset and adapting (fine-tuning) it to a new task with less data.

      For real image problems with limited data, start from a network pretrained on ImageNet and retrain only the top. This usually beats training from scratch by a wide margin.

      train_ds would typically come from keras.utils.image_dataset_from_directory("data/train", image_size=(224, 224), batch_size=32), which expects one sub-folder per class.

      28.3Sequence models: forecasting a time series Intermediate

      Definitions

      RNN / LSTM: recurrent neural networks process sequences step by step while keeping a memory (hidden state); the LSTM is a variant that remembers long-range patterns well.

      Forecasting horizon: how far ahead a forecast predicts: one step, a week, a year.

      For sequences we feed the model a window of past values and ask it to predict the next one. Keras' timeseries_dataset_from_array builds the windows for you.

      Output
      (32, 40) (32,)
      Output
      test RMSE  naive=0.260  LSTM=0.210  Conv1D=0.160
      Bug huntMy forecaster is worse than "same as last time"

      Check three things. First, normalisation: did you scale with training statistics and un-scale predictions? Second, architecture: a global pooling layer (GlobalAveragePooling1D) or a too-short window throws away when things happened, and for forecasting the most recent values matter most (Flatten or an RNN keeps the order). Third, alignment: are the targets really the next step after each window? An off-by-one shift silently trains the model to predict the present.

      Research practiceEvaluate forecasts honestly

      Split by time (never shuffle across the split), normalise with training statistics, compare against naive and seasonal-naive baselines, and if you tune hyperparameters, use TimeSeriesSplit or a rolling-origin evaluation. Multi-step forecasts degrade with the horizon, so report errors per horizon.

      28.4Custom training loops Advanced

      When fit() is not flexible enough (research on new losses, GANs, unusual schedules), write the loop yourself. It is the GradientTape pattern from Chapter 26 applied to a Keras model.

      Output

      28.5Other architectures in one table Intermediate

      Data Architecture Keras building blocks
      Images CNN, ResNet, EfficientNet, Vision Transformer Conv2D, keras.applications.*
      Sequences / time series LSTM, GRU, 1-D CNN, Transformer LSTM, GRU, Conv1D, MultiHeadAttention

      Generation VAE, GAN, diffusion custom training loops
      NoteKeras 3 and other back ends

      Keras 3 can also run on JAX or PyTorch back ends (set the KERAS_BACKEND environment variable before importing Keras). The code in this part runs on the default TensorFlow back end.

      Chapter 29Contents

      The ML research protocol: a complete worked study

      This chapter strings everything together into a protocol you can follow for a thesis chapter or a paper, and runs it end to end on a real dataset. Each step says what to do, why, and what to report. Copy the structure, swap in your data.

      The study. Can routinely measured cell-nucleus features from fine-needle aspirate images classify breast masses as malignant or benign, and which features drive the prediction? (Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer data, 569 cases, bundled with scikit-learn.)

      29.1The protocol at a glance Beginner

      Definitions

      Research protocol: a written, step-by-step plan for a study, fixed before analysis, covering the question, data, methods and how results will be judged.

      Primary metric: the single metric chosen in advance to judge success. Others are reported as secondary.

      Step Do Report
      1. Question Define the target, the unit of analysis, the population, the primary metric, and what "useful" means Objective, outcome definition, primary metric
      2. Data Document the source, variables, missingness and exclusions Data source, sample size, a table of characteristics
      3. Explore Distributions, class balance, correlations, oddities, using training data for decisions Key descriptive statistics, any data issues found
      4. Split Lock a test set away (stratified, grouped or temporal as appropriate) Split method, sizes, seed
      5. Baselines Dummy model and a simple, interpretable model Baseline performance
      6. Compare Candidate pipelines under repeated cross-validation Mean ± SD for every candidate, not just the winner
      7. Tune Hyperparameter search inside CV; nested CV if there is no test set Search space, method, chosen values
      8. Test Evaluate the final model on the test set once, with confidence intervals Test metrics with 95% CIs, confusion matrix, curves
      9. Interpret Permutation importance, PDP/SHAP, error analysis, checked for stability Top features, their direction, caveats
      10. Robustness Seeds, calibration, learning curve, subgroups, sensitivity analyses Variability and limitations
      11. Reproduce Save code, environment, seeds, model; write it up Software versions, code availability

      29.2Step 1: define the question before touching the data Beginner

      Write these down first. They stop you from moving the goalposts after seeing results.

      • Target: malignant (1) vs benign (0), from histopathology.
      • Unit of analysis: one mass per patient (so a random split is valid; with repeated measures you would group by patient).
      • Primary metric: ROC AUC (threshold-free ranking quality). Secondary: sensitivity (recall for malignant) at a threshold chosen on training data, specificity, balanced accuracy, Brier score.
      • What counts as useful: high sensitivity, because a missed cancer is costlier than a false alarm.
      Research practicePre-specify

      Writing the analysis plan (metric, split, candidate models, tuning budget) before modelling, ideally with a timestamp (OSF, a dated Git commit), is the ML equivalent of pre-registration. It is your best defence against accidental p-hacking ("trying things until something works").

      PitfallExplore with care

      Looking at the whole dataset to understand variables and spot errors is fine. Using it to choose features or thresholds is not: those choices must be made on training data. A safe habit is to split first and run detailed exploration on the training set only.

      Definitions

      Hold-out set: data set aside from all model development and used only for final evaluation (the test set).

      NoteReading these results

      The L1 penalty keeps worst radius in every resample, while near-duplicates such as worst area are included only some of the time (see "% non-zero"). Shuffling worst radius therefore hurts a lot, while shuffling a duplicate changes little. That does not make area irrelevant: the model only needed one member of that correlated group. Interpret importance at the level of groups of correlated features. In the stability table, features with the same sign in all 25 resamples are robust findings; features that appear in only some resamples (low "% non-zero") are not.

      PitfallThe test set can disagree with your plan

      The threshold was chosen to give at least 95% sensitivity on out-of-fold training predictions. On the test set, sensitivity came out lower (see the table above). The confidence interval is wide because there are only about 53 malignant test cases. This is exactly why you report CIs, and why you never quietly move the threshold after seeing test results. Report the shortfall honestly; if the target is critical, collect more data or validate the threshold on an independent cohort.

      Research practiceA results paragraph you could adapt

      "Six candidate pipelines were compared using 5 × 5 repeated stratified cross-validation on the training set (n = 426). L1-regularised logistic regression performed as well as or better than the non-linear models (CV ROC AUC 0.998; Table 2) and was selected for interpretability. After tuning by grid search, the final model achieved a ROC AUC of 0.977 (95% bootstrap CI 0.944–0.999) on the held-out test set (n = 143). At a threshold pre-specified on training data to target ≥ 95% sensitivity, test sensitivity was 0.906 (0.816–0.980) and specificity 0.989 (0.965–1.000), so the sensitivity target was not met on the test set. Across ten different random splits the test AUC ranged from 0.974 to 0.999." Every number comes from the outputs above. Copy them exactly; never round in your favour, and report targets that were missed.
